name: pdf
title: Merge or split PDFs
pitch: Join scanned pages into one PDF, or take one page out of a long one, without uploading your papers to a website. A small library does the hard part: you learn to use it, then turn it into a real command-line tool.

steps.do: Create a test folder and COPY two or three PDFs into it. Work on copies: a program in progress can overwrite a file by mistake.
steps.done: the folder holds 2 or 3 PDFs, and the originals are safe somewhere else.
steps.hint: Any PDFs will do: an invoice, a ticket, a manual. If you have none, most programs can "print to PDF".
steps.why: Working on copies is the first habit of anyone who writes programs that touch files. A bug costs you nothing when the originals are safe.

steps.do: Create a virtual environment for your project and install the pypdf library in it with pip.
steps.done: `import pypdf` works in your program without an error.
steps.hint: Look up `python3 -m venv`, then activate it and run `pip install pypdf` inside it.
steps.why: A virtual environment keeps each project's libraries apart, so installing something for one project never breaks another. pip is how Python programmers get the libraries other people wrote.

steps.do: Open one PDF with pypdf and print how many pages it has.
steps.done: the number matches what your PDF reader shows.
steps.hint: pypdf has a `PdfReader` class; its `pages` behave like a list, and `len()` works on them.
steps.why: Before changing a file, you read it. Counting pages proves your program really understands the file, and `len()` on something that isn't a plain list shows how Python reuses the same ideas everywhere.

steps.do: Merge two PDFs into a new file called merged.pdf.
steps.done: merged.pdf has the pages of both files, in order.
steps.hint: A `PdfWriter` collects pages: add every page of the first file, then of the second, then write it to a file opened in "wb" mode.
steps.why: Reading from one object and writing to another is the shape of most file tools. The "wb" mode matters: a PDF is binary data, not text.

steps.do: Merge every PDF of the folder, sorted by name, into one file.
steps.done: one file holds all of them, in alphabetical order of their names.
steps.hint: `pathlib.Path(folder).glob("*.pdf")` lists them, and `sorted()` puts them in order.
steps.why: Going from two named files to "every file in a folder" is where a script starts saving you real time. Sorting matters: the order a folder lists its files in is not guaranteed.

steps.do: Split: save one page of a PDF as its own file.
steps.hint: Same tools, the other way around: a writer with just one page in it.
steps.why: Splitting is merging backwards. Seeing that two features share the same building blocks is how you start to design programs instead of copying code.

steps.do: Split a whole PDF into one file per page.
steps.done: a 5-page PDF gives 5 files, named page_1.pdf to page_5.pdf.
steps.hint: A loop over the pages, with `enumerate()` to get each page's number, and an f-string for the file name.
steps.why: People count from 1, Python counts from 0. Every programmer meets this gap; `enumerate(pages, start=1)` is one clean way to bridge it.

steps.do: Extract a range of pages, for example 2 to 4, into a new PDF.
steps.done: the new file has exactly pages 2, 3 and 4.
steps.hint: A slice of the pages list: think about where it starts and where it stops (the stop is not included).
steps.why: Ranges are a classic source of off-by-one mistakes. Testing with a range you can check by eye is how you catch them.

steps.do: Let the user choose from the command line, without editing the code: `python pdf.py merge a.pdf b.pdf out.pdf` and `python pdf.py split a.pdf`.
steps.done: both commands work, and a wrong command prints how to use the program.
steps.hint: `sys.argv` holds the words typed after `python`; the `argparse` module does the same with a nicer help.
steps.why: Arguments turn a script you edit into a tool you use. It's the line between "my code" and "my program".

steps.do: Handle mistakes: a missing file, a file that isn't a PDF, a page number that doesn't exist, and an output file that already exists (don't overwrite it).
steps.done: each mistake prints a clear message instead of a crash, and no file is ever overwritten.
steps.hint: `try` / `except` around the risky part; `Path.exists()` before writing.
steps.why: A program for other people must survive their mistakes. A clear message tells them what to fix; a traceback only tells them your program broke.

steps.do: Optional: rotate pages, or open a password-protected PDF.
steps.done: it works on one test file.
steps.hint: Look in the pypdf documentation: pages can be rotated, and the reader can decrypt.
steps.why: Reading a library's documentation to find a feature yourself is a skill on its own, and the most useful one you can practise.
